transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-05-21
Time: 15:00 PT
Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Liam O'Connor (Redwood SE), Priya Nair (Redwood CSM), Diego Marquez (Arbora CTO), Sarah Lin (Arbora Head of ML), Tom Becker (Arbora SRE), Nina Patel (Arbora FinOps)
Shared: demo deck (https://redwood.ai/sales/decks/arbora-onboarding.pdf), pilot template sheet, security packet link noted in next steps

Quick summary: 48-min product walkthrough focused on using the Console to map per-route usage, set chargeback tags, and understand per-route cost breakdowns. Customer wants to validate chargeback model across three production routes and understand latency/cost tradeoffs before a pilot. Security and data residency touched on briefly.

Topics: per-route dashboards, usage lanes, tag-based allocation, estimated cost per 1M tokens, dedicated vs hosted routing, SSO/SSO gaps, pilot scope and timelines

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya: Alright, thanks everyone for joining. uh this is Maya from Redwood, AE on the account. we thought we'd walk through the Console's usage lanes and how you can get a per-route cost breakout. Liam will do the demo, I'll jump in on pricing.
[00:18] Diego: Great, thanks. quick context — we run three main inference routes: chat-assistant, email-summarize, and clinical-extract. we want per-route bills so finance can charge teams. also latency SLOs differ, so we need to see cost/latency tradeoffs.
[00:35] Liam: Perfect. and just to confirm, do you have existing tags on requests today? like team, env, or product?
[00:42] Sarah: we have an X-team header and sometimes a project id in metadata. not consistent though, which is why the dashboard sounds useful.
[00:48] Liam: ok that makes sense. I'll start share screen — tell me if the visual is fuzzy. (screen share starts)
[01:05] Liam: so this is the Console landing page. the feature we call "usage lanes" groups routes into lanes based on tags or routing keys. you can see we have an example lane here: production chat, low-latency lane, and batch lane.
[01:30] Liam: if I click into the production chat lane — this shows the per-route time series for tokens, request count, and importantly the token-level cost estimate. notice the right panel — model variant breakdown, and the average latency bucketed by hour.
[01:52] Tom: mhm, i'm scanning — how are you attributing GPU usage vs host overhead? our infra team cares about model hot cache vs idle cost.
[02:02] Liam: good call. the Console's cost model uses per-token compute estimates fed from runtime telemetry — it includes GPU kernel time for generation and a small infra overhead constant. we expose both as separate columns in the export so you can split GPU compute vs platform overhead. the numbers are heuristics but we let you calibrate them with a short benchmark.
[02:28] Sarah: can you show an example of calibrating? we run mixed contexts 128–2048 tokens so the distribution matters.
[02:36] Liam: yeah — under Optimize > Benchmarks you can run a sequence-length profile. we take sample traces and produce a multiplier table per model and seq-len bucket. I'll run a small synthetic now — bear with me — (click) — ok results coming up. see this chart: cost per 1k tokens by seq bucket for the open llama-v2-7B quantized variant.
[03:05] Diego: interesting, so that explains why chat spikes on longer threads. what about caching? we have some prefix reuse in the assistant route.
[03:13] Liam: we surfaced prefix/KV cache savings as an adjustable factor. if you enable prefix caching on the route, the effective token count drops and the Console updates the cost projection in real time. you can toggle caching and see projected savings like 18–34% depending on reuse.
[03:31] Nina: from finance perspective, we need a monthly export that aligns with our billing periods and maps to our 3 cost centers. is that possible?
[03:38] Liam: absolutely — routing tags map to cost centers. you can configure multiple tag rules, plus fallback rules for untagged requests. the export has columns: timestamp, route, tag-set, token_count, estimated_compute_cost, infra_overhead, total_cost. you can pipe that CSV to your chargeback tool.
[03:58] Mia: (interruption) sorry — this is Maya — does the export include the model variant? we sometimes move models and need to reconcile.
[04:05] Liam: yes — model id and model version are columns. also we include the serving mode (hosted/dedicated/private) for each request, so you can reconcile reserved capacity costs.
[04:18] Diego: quick question on private deployments — we might put clinical-extract on-prem. would that route show in the Console with same metrics?
[04:26] Maya: yes — with Redwood Private the control plane in your VPC forwards telemetry. the Console still receives aggregated metrics; the only difference is the compute cost column will reflect on-prem accounting where you can insert your own cost-per-GPU figure.
[04:40] Tom: and how do you handle PII or PHI — we need to know if anything leaves our network during telemetry collection.
[04:48] Priya: good question — we have a telemetry redaction option and a host-side aggregator that strips payloads. the security packet we shared in next steps details that, and there's a deployable collector for air-gapped setups.
[05:02] Diego: ok please send that.
[05:06] Liam: moving back to dashboards — here's the per-route flame chart, it aggregates the token spend by route and by model variant. you can click to drill down to the hour level. notice how this lane compares: chat-assistant uses more short-lived tokens but higher QPS; clinical-extract has lower QPS but longer seqs.
[05:30] Sarah: are there built-in SLO alerts? like if latency crosses 250ms P95 for the low-latency lane?
[05:37] Liam: yes, under Alerts you can create SLO monitors per lane or per route. they can trigger Slack, PagerDuty, or webhook. also you can create cost anomaly alerts if a route's daily spend deviates from the rolling 7-day baseline.
[05:52] Nina: do you show amortized reserved capacity costs? e.g., we buy dedicated nodes so our per-token compute cost is lower but amortized monthly.
[06:01] Liam: we do. in the billing model selector you can pick between on-demand unit costs or reserved amortized lines. the export will then apply the reserved allocation across matched routes by a policy (equal weight, usage-weighted, or custom).
[06:17] Diego: can we map reserved capacity to multiple projects? some of our GPUs are shared across teams.
[06:22] Liam: yes you can apportion reserved capacity across tags. there's also a priority assignment for guaranteed throughput lanes.
[06:29] Sarah: show me a demo of creating a custom lane for 'clinical-prod' that pins to a dedicated pool and enforces a fallback to hosted if capacity exhausted.
[06:38] Liam: sure — create lane -> name = clinical-prod -> add tag rule project=clinical -> assign pool = 'dedicated-gpu-b'. then rollout policy -> primary pool = dedicated-gpu-b, fallback = hosted-medium, failover threshold = 85% util. save — and here's the simulated rollout graph that shows expected latency increase on fallback.
[07:05] Tom: that sim is helpful. what about cost during fallback — do we see both reserved and on-demand charges?
[07:12] Liam: the Console reports blended per-token cost when mixed pools are used and also a separate line-level view that shows how many tokens served from each pool during the window.
[07:23] Maya: quick interruption — pricing note: reserved pools have a monthly commitment; we provide both a capacity-based and a per-token blended option in the contract. i'll follow up with the sheet.
[07:34] Diego: good. back to tagging — we have messy headers. can your routing rules extract project IDs from JSON payloads or nested metadata?
[07:44] Liam: yes, the routing rules support JSONPath and regex extractions. you can also fallback to IP-mapping or JWT claims. we recommend adding a lightweight client SDK interceptor to guarantee tags at the client side — that makes chargeback more reliable.
[08:00] Sarah: we use Envoy sidecars, could we enforce header injection there?
[08:04] Liam: absolutely, many customers do header enrichment at the proxy layer. Redwood's routing accepts those headers.
[08:09] Diego: can you show the per-route cost view for an org with mixed hosted/dedicated last month?
[08:15] Liam: pulling a sample tenant... ok here's an example: three routes, stacked area chart. the UI also has a table view with sort by total_cost. i'll switch to table. you can see tokens, model, pool, est_compute, infra_overhead, total.
[08:36] Nina: does the table support annotations? like tagging a row as 'compliance hold' so finance can exclude it?
[08:43] Liam: you can mark rows and create an annotation tag; annotation isn't retroactively applied unless you run a reallocation job. there is a bulk reclassify tool for historical windows.
[08:55] Sarah: about model variants — when we roll a smaller quantized model to save cost, is there an A/B view for quality/regression?
[09:03] Liam: yes — we integrate with Redwood Optimize. you can define an eval set and run side-by-side quality metrics and cost deltas. the Console will then show a quality vs cost scatter and a recommended break-even point.
[09:18] Diego: that sounds useful. if we run the pilot with two routes first — chat-assistant and email-summarize — what metrics should we collect?
[09:26] Liam: primary: tokens, latency percentiles (p50/p95/p99), inference errors, and quality score from your eval set (if available). also measure prefix reuse ratio for chat. we'll provide a pilot workbook.
[09:38] Maya: i'll attach the pilot workbook after the call.
[09:42] Tom: switching topics — security review: SSO, RBAC mapping to org groups, and audit logs — do you store full request payloads in logs?
[09:52] Priya: default logs are metadata-only; we have a configurable opt-in for payload logs which you can route to your private S3. for SOC2 customers we recommend the host-side aggregator that strips payloads and pushes only hashes. RBAC integrates with SAML/Okta and you can map roles to actions in the Console.
[10:10] Diego: fine. is there sample ACL template?
[10:13] Priya: yes — included in the security packet link.
[10:15] Sarah: does the Console show cost-per-intent or cost-per-customer if we pass customer_id?
[10:22] Liam: yes, if you include customer_id in tags we can group by it. the UI has a 'group by' dropdown: route, tag key, model, customer_id. that lets you create reports like cost per customer across routes.
[10:33] Nina: our finance team will want to run a 6-month projection — can the Console project spend if we apply a 20% growth assumption?
[10:41] Liam: there's a forecast tab — you can apply growth curves and seasonality and it outputs a monthly projection with confidence intervals. it uses trend extrapolation and your planned model changes if provided.
[10:54] Diego: any limitations on retention for usage data? we need 12 months.
[11:00] Maya: retention tiers are configurable; default is 90 days for high-res and 12 months for aggregated. on enterprise plan we can extend to multi-year.
[11:09] Sarah: ok, towards the end — can you demo creating a saved report that our finance team can schedule weekly?
[11:16] Liam: create report -> name = Arbora weekly chargeback -> group by = route, primary tag = project -> columns = tokens, est_compute, infra_overhead, total_cost -> schedule weekly Mondays. save. and here's the subscription config to send to email or S3.
[11:39] Tom: good. on the pilot, what's a minimal data sample you need? we can export last 2 weeks of traffic.
[11:46] Liam: 2 weeks is great. ideally include both peak and off-peak windows and a CSV with header mapping for any custom fields. we'll use that to run the initial calibration.
[11:57] Diego: one more question about anomalies — do you backfill anomalies when you correct a tag mapping error?
[12:03] Liam: yes, we provide a reclassification job. it will re-run cost attribution across the selected window and update the saved report. we keep an audit trail of changes.
[12:14] Maya: ok, want to quickly walk through an example export? i'll trigger a sample CSV from the demo tenant.
[12:20] Liam: sure. exporting now ... the file includes route_id, timestamp, request_id, token_count, model_id, pool, est_compute_cost, infra_overhead, total_cost, tag_json. (file pops up) you can see a couple of rows here.
[12:40] Sarah: ok that looks like what we'd need.
[12:43] Diego: what's typical delta between Console estimate and actual invoice? we need to reconcile to cents.
[12:50] Liam: typically within 2–6% after calibration. big deltas come from sequence-length distribution shifts or significant prefix reuse. that's why we recommend a short benchmark/run to calibrate the model and, for tight reconciliation, use the reserved capacity amortization option.
[13:10] Nina: what about multi-region routing? our EU customers must serve in eu-west only for data residency.
[13:17] Liam: lanes can be region-constrained. we route by policy and you can enforce region-only execution, and the Console will break down regional costs separately.
[13:28] Diego: could you give an example of a rule that enforces EU-only for certain routes?
[13:32] Liam: rule: IF route in [clinical-extract] AND header geo=EU THEN pool=eu-dedicated; else block or fallback to hosted-eu. it's a simple policy builder in the UI.
[13:45] Sarah: are there rate limits per lane? we don't want a noisy consumer to blast dedicated nodes.
[13:50] Liam: yes, per-lane quotas and burst tokens are configurable; you can also throttle or reject requests.
[13:57] Diego: ok this is covering most questions. any objections from the team?
[14:02] Tom: none here. looks promising.
[14:05] Maya: all right, final recap and next steps: we'll email pricing options and reserved capacity details; Liam will prepare the pilot runbook and a benchmark plan; Priya will send security packet and onboarding checklist; Arbora will share two weeks of traffic sample and the CSV mapping. schedule pilot kickoff for early July.
[14:27] Diego: sounds good. thanks everyone.
[14:30] Maya: thanks all — end call.

Notes on transcript quality: automatic transcription had a few mis-attributed speakers near the end during crosstalk; technical terms occasionally misrecognized (e.g., KV cache as K-V cash in one spot).
